strategy.summary: Reproduce the sigma_max gradient crash on rectangular matrices by applying the PR's test additions on the buggy commit 008eb3af3029 and running the sigma_max grad configs in cvxpy/tests/test_grad.py. The buggy revision should raise ValueError from the gradient path (LA.svd with full_matrices=True gives misaligned inner dimensions). The fixed revision should compute the gradient and pass the finite-difference comparison. The defect is pure Python and deterministic linear algebra, so it needs no compiled build and no special platform.

pip_packages: cvxpy (checked out at 008eb3af3029, installed editable via pip install -e .)
build_commands: git apply test_grad_pr3246.diff  # apply only the test_grad.py hunk from the PR
pinned_because: All six dependency constraints are documented in README.md (kind explicit, era_ceiling null), so the versions above are the documented floors; no era-inferred pins are applied.
NumPy >=2.0.0 is documented and relevant because the SVD full_matrices behaviour is the trigger path; the environment does not pin an upper bound because the evidence gives none.

strategy.reproducing_test: cvxpy/tests/test_grad.py: the new AtomTestConfig entries 'sigma_max_nonsquare' (shape (2, 3)) and 'sigma_max_tall' (shape (4, 2)), both with the 'unrestricted' domain, selected by -k sigma_max alongside the existing square sigma_max (3, 3) config.
strategy.success_criterion: On the buggy revision (008eb3af3029 with the test diff applied), the sigma_max_nonsquare and sigma_max_tall configs error out with a ValueError raised from sigma_max._grad when the gradient is requested, so those test IDs FAIL. On the fixed revision (the PR head with LA.svd(values[0], full_matrices=False) and the U[:, 0:1] @ V[0:1, :] gradient), the same test IDs run the gradient, match the finite-difference reference within the harness tolerance, and PASS. The square (3, 3) config should pass on both revisions.
strategy.numerical_probe: Compare the analytic gradient U[:,0:1] @ V[0:1,:] of the largest singular value against a central finite-difference gradient on a (2,3) and a (4,2) random matrix; the harness performs this comparison.

input_output_examples.expected_output: gradient computed without error, matching the numerical gradient to machine precision

risks: The transition depends on the test harness reaching sigma_max._grad. Confirm the test method calls .grad (or the gradient-check helper) for every AtomTestConfig, not only the square case; if it does not, the buggy revision may not fail.

Forward solves for sigma_max go through an SDP reformulation, so a solver capable of SDP must be available (Clarabel or SCS, both documented). If the default solver is unavailable, the test may error before reaching _grad, which would look like a failure on both revisions.
Machine-precision tolerance is described only qualitatively in the evidence (no numeric value stated), so the harness's own tolerance decides pass/fail on the fixed revision; this is not pinned here.
No concrete input matrices or expected gradient values are given beyond the shapes (2, 3) and (4, 2); the random inputs in the harness are what matter.

The failure is a shape error, not a numerical one, so it should appear on any platform (Linux, macOS, Windows) and with any BLAS. No architecture-specific or sanitizer-specific behaviour is evidenced, so no special platform is required.

oracle.reference_source: finite-difference numerical gradient computed by the cvxpy test_grad harness
oracle.why: The PR states the analytic gradient matches the numerical gradient to machine precision, but gives no numeric tolerance, so the harness's own tolerance is the oracle.

strategy.fails_on_buggy: On the buggy revision, LA.svd(values[0]) returns full U and V with mismatched inner dimensions for rectangular inputs, so the gradient matmul raises ValueError when .grad is called; the test errors and therefore fails.
strategy.passes_on_fixed: With full_matrices=False the U and V factors have aligned inner dimensions and the rank-one gradient U[:,0:1] @ V[0:1,:] is computed without error, matching the finite-difference reference, so the test passes.
